summary: Describes an RTP payload format for retransmissions, which recover lost packets in real-time applications with relaxed delay limits. Retransmitted packets are sent in a separate stream from the original, and receivers are assumed to send feedback. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4588 defines a way to resend lost RTP packets without mixing them into the original RTP sequence. A retransmission uses a separate stream and carries the original packet's sequence number so the receiver can identify it.

questions: what is the rtx payload type
subtitle: A payload format for requesting and sending RTP packet retransmissions in a separate stream.

tldr.problem: Lost RTP packets can reduce media quality, but retransmitting them in the original stream would disrupt sequence numbers and RTCP statistics.
tldr.mechanism: A sender retransmits in a separate RTP stream, including the original sequence number in a two-octet payload header. Receivers request lost packets using RTCP feedback, usually NACK.
tldr.outcome: The format supports unicast and small multicast groups when delay bounds allow retransmission. Original and retransmitted traffic together must remain within congestion limits.

today: RFC 4588 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2006. It is designed for use with the RTP/AVPF profile in RFC 4585; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: When RTP Retransmission Is Useful
sections.content:
Packet loss can degrade media delivered with the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). Possible repair techniques include forward error correction, retransmission, and interleaving. The appropriate choice depends on how much delay the application can tolerate.

Retransmission is generally unsuitable for interactive conferencing that must keep end-to-end delay to a few hundred milliseconds. Streaming applications may accept delays of several seconds, so they can request lost packets before playback. This format assumes receiver feedback, particularly the RTCP feedback defined by the RTP/AVPF profile in RFC 4585, and is intended for unicast and small multicast groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Retransmission helps when an application can wait for a missing packet to be sent again. It is aimed at streaming with relaxed delay bounds, not applications that need immediate delivery.

sections.title: Why Retransmissions Use a Separate Stream
sections.content:
The design preserves ordinary RTP and RTCP behavior and lets receivers detect which original packets were lost from gaps in sequence numbers. Sending an unchanged packet again in the original stream would corrupt RTCP statistics because sequence numbers would not increase normally. Sending retransmissions in the same stream under another payload type would make original packet loss harder to identify.

RFC 4588 therefore uses a separate retransmission stream and includes the original sequence number in each retransmitted packet. The streams may use separate RTP sessions (session-multiplexing) or different SSRC values in one session (SSRC-multiplexing). Both methods SHOULD be supported for unicast. Multicast MUST use session-multiplexing because receivers cannot reliably associate streams using SSRC-multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage: The retransmission stream has its own sequence numbers, so it does not alter the original stream's packet accounting. Each resent packet also identifies the original sequence number it replaces.

sections.title: The Retransmission Packet Format
sections.content:
A retransmission packet contains an RTP header followed by a two-octet payload header and the original RTP packet payload. The payload header contains the Original Sequence Number (OSN), which MUST equal the sequence number of the original packet. The RTP sequence number increases normally in the retransmission stream, and its timestamp MUST be the original packet's timestamp.

The dynamic payload type is mapped to the original payload type through SDP. The timestamp clock rate must match the original payload type. Marker bit, CSRC count, and CSRC list are copied from the original header. Header extensions SHOULD be repeated, and original RTP padding MUST be removed before constructing the retransmission packet. A sender MAY retransmit data encoded at a lower rate if receivers can still decode dependent packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The RTP header identifies the retransmission stream. A two-octet OSN then identifies the original packet, followed by that packet's payload.

sections.title: Matching Streams and Requesting Packets
sections.content:
A retransmission session MUST correspond to exactly one original session. The original and retransmission streams MUST use the same RTCP CNAME. With session-multiplexing, a receiver pairs streams with the same SSRC in their separate sessions. With SSRC-multiplexing, it first compares CNAME values and may resolve ambiguity when a requested packet is retransmitted.

Receivers SHOULD use AVPF NACK feedback to request missing packets, and NACKs MUST be sent only for the original stream. A receiver should consider whether a retransmission can arrive in time, estimate round-trip time, and allow for packet reordering before requesting it. It may repeat a NACK after a timer based on observed round-trip time.

For the same sequence number in multiple original streams, a receiver MUST avoid having two outstanding requests before it resolves SSRC association. This ambiguity cannot be avoided in multicast, which is why multicast cannot use SSRC-multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver matches a retransmission to its original stream, then asks for missing original packets with NACK feedback. It allows time for reordered packets before deciding that a packet is lost.

sections.title: Congestion, SDP, and RTSP
sections.content:
In a best-effort network, packet loss may result from congestion. The acceptable packet rate and bitrate therefore include both original and retransmitted data. A sender SHOULD NOT retransmit in a best-effort environment without reducing the original stream's rate, for example by encoding at a lower rate. It MAY selectively retransmit important packets and ignore other NACKs. If congestion cannot be controlled, retransmission SHOULD NOT be used.

The RTP retransmission payload type is named rtx. SDP uses required parameters rate and apt, which maps a retransmission payload type to its original payload type. Optional rtx-time states how long the sender keeps an original packet available, in milliseconds. Retransmission streams SHOULD NOT be cached, and RTSP PLAY and PAUSE SHOULD NOT control retransmission packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Retransmissions consume bandwidth in addition to original packets, so a sender must account for both. SDP can state which original payload a retransmission format belongs to and how long packets remain available.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General RTP security considerations apply. Without authentication, altered RTCP can trigger unnecessary retransmissions, altered retransmission packets can affect a decoder, and replayed packets can distort timing measurements or overflow a receiver buffer. Confidentiality requires encrypting the original payload; the two-octet retransmission header need not be encrypted.

If the original stream uses cryptographic protection, the retransmission stream MUST receive equivalent protection. Reusing the same key for both streams may create security problems such as two-time pads. The RFC notes that the SRTP specification available when it was written did not provide all the services needed for this payload format.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect RTCP feedback and retransmission packets against alteration and replay. If the original stream is protected, the retransmission stream must receive equivalent protection, with care not to reuse keys in a way that weakens security.
